title: Building this site with an AI-assisted feedback loop
summary: How implementation, browser review and content structure evolved together, and why the portfolio keeps more detail than the CV.
lead: My background is backend and AI engineering, and I wanted a site I could maintain without turning frontend polish into a side project. I used ChatGPT and Cursor to implement and refine it, and the part that mattered most was not the generation but the feedback: concrete observations, browser review and verification after each change.

diagram.chart:
graph LR
    DATA["src/db/*.json"] --> SITE["Website: Home and About"]
    DATA --> BUILD["scripts/build_resume.py"]
    BUILD --> PDF["public/resume: PDF, preview, manifest"]
    SITE --> CHECK["Visual and behavior review"]
    PDF --> CHECK
diagram.caption: Profile data is the single source of truth. The website and the CV are both generated from it, with selection flags deciding what the shorter document includes.

sections.title: Make feedback concrete enough to act on
paragraphs: The original article describes an iterative loop: edit the implementation, view it in the browser, capture what looks wrong, give more specific feedback and repeat. How good the result is depends on how good that feedback is.

A request such as making a page look better leaves too much open. A screenshot and one specific observation make the next change small: a heading has too little contrast, the content column is too wide, or the mobile header overflows the viewport.

The best iterations keep decisions that already work. In the latest profile refresh the emerald light theme and the blue and slate dark theme stayed in place, and typography, spacing and hierarchy carried the improvement.

sections.title: Give content a source of truth
paragraphs: Profile, experience, project, skill, education and certificate data live separately from the components that render them. Updating the About page becomes a content change instead of a search for repeated text in markup.

The same data now feeds the CV renderer. Explicit selection flags decide which entries belong in the shorter PDF, so the website can keep an older project without forcing every project into a fixed-length resume.

sections.title: Treat the portfolio and the resume as different documents
paragraphs: The refresh exposed a real mistake: choosing a short project list for the CV also removed older projects from the About page. The fix was architectural as well as editorial. About shows the full catalog and the PDF uses its own selection.

The two surfaces serve different readers. Someone scanning a CV needs the most relevant evidence quickly. Someone visiting the portfolio may want the history, the implementation detail and a full project write-up.

sections.title: Review behavior as well as screenshots
paragraphs: Visual review covered desktop and narrow mobile widths, navigation, theme persistence, section anchors and the PDF download path. It found a header overflow that was not visible on desktop, and it confirmed that the downloaded PDF matched the generated file.

A passing build and focused lint checks are useful evidence, but the repository still has older lint and type issues, and the build configuration skips those checks. A successful build does not mean every check is clean.

sections.title: Keep publishing and privacy explicit
paragraphs: The public CV carries professional profile links and no personal phone number or email address. Draft files and local review artifacts stay outside the published asset directory, and the old public PDF was removed from the source tree.

Publishing a corrected file does not erase Git history or copies people already downloaded, which is why artifacts are reviewed before they are pushed. The result is less a page generated by AI than a publishing workflow where content, design, privacy and verification each have a place.
